description:
src/async_crl.rs:64 / src/async_ocsp.rs:64: `return checker.check_revocation(cert, issuer)` is a synchronous call to OcspChecker::check_revocation / CrlChecker::check_revocation from inside an async fn. The check includes DER parsing AND signature verification (RSA-2048: ~1ms; RSA-4096: ~5ms; ECDSA-P256: ~0.5ms; PKCS-1.5 with SHA-512: similar).

On a multi-threaded tokio runtime this is acceptable — the worker thread blocks for a few ms, other workers continue. On a single-threaded runtime (current_thread, smol's single executor, embedded async runtimes), this stalls ALL tasks for the same duration. A consumer choosing tokio's current_thread for a memory-tight build (no work-stealing scheduler overhead) discovers latency cliffs under concurrent revocation checks.

The module rustdoc acknowledges this: 'CRL parsing and signature verification stay synchronous because they do no I/O.' That justifies the design (don't introduce CPU-bound futures via spawn_blocking on a hot path that doesn't need it), but the cost is invisible to consumers who don't read the rationale.

Recommendation: add a Limitations note to the crate-level docstring naming this explicitly. Something like 'Signature verification runs on the calling task. On single-threaded async runtimes, callers should expect per-cert latency of a few ms; if this is a problem, wrap the call in tokio::task::spawn_blocking.' This is a documentation fix, not an API change.

The deeper fix — make signature verification a separate async-friendly callback — is out of scope: it would force every SignatureVerifier impl to wrap synchronous primitives in Future-returning machinery, for no benefit on multi-threaded runtimes.
title: Sync verifier.check_revocation called inside async fn blocks executor thread for ms-scale CPU
